'''''Arithmetica Universalis''''' ("Universal Arithmetic") is a [[mathematics]] text by [[Isaac Newton]]. Written in [[Latin language|Latin]], it was edited and published by [[William Whiston]], Newton's successor as [[Lucasian Professor of Mathematics]] at the University of Cambridge. The ''Arithmetica'' was based on Newton's lecture notes.
==Publication history==
Whiston's original edition was published in 1707. It was translated into English by [[Joseph Raphson]], who published it in 1720 as the ''Universal Arithmetick''. [[John Machin]] published a second Latin edition in 1722.
==Lack of credit for the writer==
None of these editions credit Newton as author; Newton was unhappy with the publication of the ''Arithmetica'', and so refused to have his name appear. In fact, when Whiston's edition was published, Newton was so upset he considered purchasing all of the copies so he could destroy them.<ref>{{cite journal
 | last = Whitrow | first = G. J.
 | date = January 1989
 | doi = 10.1098/rsnr.1989.0006
 | issue = 1
 | journal = Notes and Records of the Royal Society of London
 | pages = 71–92
 | publisher = The Royal Society
 | title = Newton's role in the history of Mathematics*
 | volume = 43}} See Section III, p. 79.</ref>

==Content==
The ''Arithmetica'' touches on algebraic notation, arithmetic, the relationship between [[geometry]] and [[algebra]], and the solution of equations. Newton also applied [[René Descartes|Descartes]]' [[Descartes' rule of signs|rule of signs]] to [[imaginary numbers|imaginary]] roots. He also offered, without proof, a rule to determine the number of imaginary roots of polynomial equations. A rigorous proof of Newton's counting formula for equations up to and including the fifth degree was published by [[James Joseph Sylvester]] in 1864.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sylvester |first1=J.J. |title=Algebraical Researches, containing a disquisition on Newton's Rule for the Discovery of Imaginary Roots, and an allied Rule applicable to a particular class of Equations, together with a complete invariantive determination of the character of the Roots of the General Equation of the fifth Degree, &c. |journal=Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society |date=1864-04-06 |volume=154 |pages=580–591 |bibcode=1864RSPT..154..579S |url=https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.44429/page/n617/ |access-date=29 October 2023}}</ref>
